newsitem.title: CHAD: Chad holds parliamentary runoff elections.
newsitem.headline: Chad holds parliamentary runoff elections.

text.p: Chad holds parliamentary run-offs on Sunday with President Idriss Deby and his supporters hoping to get at least 26 seats to ensure a majority in the new 125-member parliament.

With both the opposition and the ruling party calling for a high turnout in the polls for 68 seats, the head of the Independent National Electoral Commission CENI called on Saturday for the authorities to remain neutral.

CENI head Pascal Yoadimnadji said in a statement broadcast on state radio and television that the country's administration, army and traditional chiefs should not interfere in polling -- "on pain of scrapping of results".
Final results from the January 5 first round released by the appeal court credited Deby's Patriotic Salvation Movement with 37 seats against a total of 20 for various other parties.
Deby, a former guerrilla leader from the Moslem north, seized power in a 1990 French-backed coup after decades of civil war or conflict with Libya.
After repeated electoral delays, he won a multi-party presidential election in July in a runoff against fellow general Wadal Abdelkader Kamougue from the largely Christian south.
Chad, a sprawling former French colony on the fringes of the Sahara desert, previously had a 57-member interim assembly under a 1993 transitional charter.
The appeal court scrapped votes cast by many of the country's nomads in the first round of the parliamentary poll.
The nomad vote was a source of dispute during last year's presidential election, with the opposition denouncing multiple or under-age voting.
Sources close to the commission said that nomads, who number an estimated 300,000 of the country's more than six million people, would not be allowed to vote in Sunday's second round.
The ruling party, in a statement on state radio on Saturday, denounced the various decisions concerning the nomad vote as "illegal and contrary to the reality of the country".
"The ruling party will do everything it can to restore the nomads their rights," the statement added.
Polling in the mainly Moslem or animist nation starts at 6 a.m. (0600 GMT) and closes at 6 p.m. (1800 GMT).
The commission said vote counting would start immediately after polling stations shut and would take place in the presence of party and candidates' representatives.
Past experience suggests it could be several days before the first results are out.
